implementation_notes: Ruby's Enumerable module gives every collection the operation: map (aliased collect) returns a new array containing the block's results, and because Array, Hash, Range, Set and any object defining each include the module, contexts inherit the operation rather than declaring it. Mapping a Hash yields [key, value] pairs, which is where hash mapping differs from list mapping, and Enumerable#filter_map/sum/group_by sit beside it. Core Ruby has no Maybe or Result container - absence is nil and failures are exceptions, handled with the safe-navigation operator and explicit nil checks, or with a library (dry-monads' Maybe/Result) when the named operation is wanted. Keep the eager form the default and switch to a lazy enumerator for large or unbounded sources.
code_sketch:
names = people.map(&:display_name)                   # new Array, one call per element
pairs = config.map { |k, v| [k.upcase, v.to_i] }.to_h  # Hash yields pairs

# no built-in Maybe: nil stays nil explicitly
city = user&.address&.city

# dry-monads supplies Maybe/Result with .map when a real context is wanted
pitfalls: Hash#map passes a single [key, value] array to a one-parameter block, so h.map { |k| ... } silently receives and returns pairs - destructure, or use transform_values.
Every stage is eager and allocates an Array, so a long chain over a big collection pays per stage; Enumerator::Lazy is the deferred form.
nil is not a context: &:symbol shorthand raises NoMethodError on a nil element (people.map(&:display_name) with a nil member), so absence needs explicit nil handling or compact.

variants.name: Enumerator::Lazy#map (deferred mapping)
variants.implementation_notes: #lazy turns the same map into a deferred operation: it returns an Enumerator::Lazy, documented as 'a special type of Enumerator, that allows constructing chains of operations without evaluating them immediately', which redefines most Enumerable methods - map and collect included - so stages build a chain and nothing is evaluated until a non-redefined method or an explicit force/to_a/first/take consumes it. That makes an unbounded source (an infinite range, a file read line by line) mappable, and a later first/take stops the upstream work. Use it for large or infinite inputs and long chains; the eager form stays simpler and is usually faster for small in-memory collections.
variants.code_sketch:
first_five = (1..Float::INFINITY).lazy
  .map { |n| n * n }              # nothing computed yet
  .select(&:even?)
  .first(5)                       # pulls only until five survivors

File.foreach('huge.log').lazy
  .map { |line| line.split(' ', 2).first }
  .first(3)
pitfalls: A lazy chain without a terminal computes nothing, and Enumerator::Lazy#map called without a block raises ArgumentError where the eager version would return an Enumerator.
Laziness re-runs the upstream work on each traversal and hides when side effects happen, which makes debugging harder than the eager chain.
Only the redefined methods stay lazy: calling a plain Enumerable method (sort, group_by) in the middle forces the whole chain.
